notes.meaning: Jonathan invited his young armor-bearer to cross the valley and secretly attack a Philistine outpost. He chose not to tell his father, King Saul, who likely would have forbidden the dangerous plan. Jonathan stepped forward in bold faith while his father sat inactive.

King Saul was resting under a pomegranate tree near Gibeah with only about six hundred soldiers left in his army. He stayed safely in his camp rather than confronting the Philistine invaders. His small force showed how weak and desperate Israel's military position appeared.

A priest named Ahijah was with Saul, wearing the priestly vest called an ephod to seek God's guidance. Ahijah came from the family line of Eli, a priesthood that God had previously judged and rejected. Meanwhile, none of Saul's soldiers knew that Jonathan had slipped away.

To reach the Philistine outpost, Jonathan had to pass between two sharp, steep rock cliffs. One cliff stood on the north side facing Michmash, and the other stood on the south side facing Geba. Their names were Bozez, which means shining, and Seneh, which means thorny.

Jonathan urged his helper to move forward against these pagan enemies who did not belong to God's covenant. He expressed confidence that the Lord can rescue his people through a tiny handful just as easily as through an army. True faith relies entirely on God's strength rather than human numbers.

The armor-bearer responded with complete loyalty and courage. He told Jonathan to carry out whatever he had in mind, promising to follow him wherever he went. Having a faithful companion who shares our trust in God brings great strength in hard times.

Jonathan explained their plan to cross over and show themselves openly to the Philistine sentries. Rather than sneaking in secretly, they would give the enemy guards an opportunity to respond. Jonathan wanted God to guide their actions through what the guards said next.

Jonathan asked God for a clear sign to show whether they should advance. If the guards told them to wait where they were, they would stay put and defend themselves. But if the guards dared them to climb up, Jonathan would take that invite as proof that God had given them victory.

The two men stepped into view at the base of the cliff. The Philistine guards mocked them, joking that the Israelites were finally crawling out of their hiding holes to find food. The guards looked down on them with pride and felt no danger at all.

The guards shouted down from the cliff, telling Jonathan and his helper to come up so they could teach them a lesson. Hearing those exact words, Jonathan knew God had given the promised sign. He told his companion to follow him because the Lord had already handed over the enemy.

Jonathan scrambled up the steep rock on his hands and knees, with his armor-bearer climbing right behind him. Jonathan struck down the surprised Philistines as soon as he reached the top, and his helper finished them off. God gave them sudden strength and speed to overwhelm the outpost.

In that opening clash, the two men killed about twenty Philistine soldiers. The entire fight took place in a tiny space about the size of half an acre of plowed field. The sudden loss of their outer guard post sent shockwaves through the enemy camp.

Sudden dread swept through the entire Philistine camp, reaching the raiding bands and the main army. At that exact moment the ground shook, and God caused a supernatural panic to spread among them. God showed that he alone holds power over both the earth and the hearts of men.

Saul's lookouts at Gibeah looked across the valley and saw the huge Philistine army falling apart. The enemy troops were scattering in every direction and beating down one another in total confusion. It became obvious to the watchmen that a major disaster had struck the invaders.

Saul realized that someone from his camp must have launched a surprise raid. He ordered an immediate muster of his six hundred men to find out who was absent. When the roll was called, only Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.

Saul instructed Ahijah the priest to bring the sacred symbol of God's presence so they could seek divine counsel. The traditional Hebrew text states that Saul asked for the ark of God. Saul wanted to know whether his army should advance and enter the battle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars follow the ancient Greek translation, which reads 'bring the ephod' instead of the ark, because the Ark was resting at Kiriath-jearim and priests used the ephod to seek God's will.

notes.meaning: While Saul was still talking with the priest, the sounds of chaos in the enemy camp grew louder and wilder. Saul grew impatient and told the priest to pull his hand back and stop inquiring of God. Saul chose to rush into action rather than wait for the Lord's full answer.

Saul gathered his men and marched out to the battlefield. When they arrived, they found the Philistine army in complete disarray, with soldiers turning their swords against their own allies. God used the enemy's own weapons to destroy them.

A group of Hebrews had previously been held by the Philistines or forced into their ranks. When these men saw the panic, they turned against their captors and joined Saul and Jonathan. Those who had been trapped among the enemy regained their freedom and stood with their brothers.

Many Israelites had earlier fled in terror to hide in the caves and hills of Ephraim. When word reached them that the Philistines were running away, they came out of their hiding spots and joined the chase. A renewed sense of hope gave courage to people who had previously been frozen with fear.

Scripture emphasizes that the Lord himself delivered Israel on that day. The fighting pushed past Beth-aven as the enemy retreated westward across the hill country. God deserves all the praise for saving his people, even though he worked through human fighters.

Even though Israel was winning, the soldiers were completely exhausted from severe hunger. Saul had placed a solemn curse on anyone who tasted food before evening, demanding personal revenge on his enemies. His foolish demand took away the army's strength right in the middle of a great victory.

The pursuing army marched into a wooded area where wild honey was lying on the ground. In that region, wild bees often built their hives in hollow trees and rock crevices. God placed sweet refreshment right in front of the weary soldiers.

When the troops entered the woods, they saw streams of fresh honey dripping from the trees. Even though the men were starving, not one person ate any because they were terrified of Saul's curse. A harsh, unwise command kept the men from enjoying the good food God had provided.
